opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the intuition is appealing, right? If a task pays a lot in the human labor market, it must be hard, and if it's hard, maybe AI will struggle with it. But I think there are a few reasons to be careful with that.

First, market price reflects a bunch of things that aren't really about the cognitive difficulty of the task. It reflects scarcity of people with the right credentials, licensing requirements, liability, how much trust and accountability you need from the person doing it, bargaining power, regulation, all sorts of institutional factors. A lawyer reviewing a contract gets paid a lot partly because someone has to be on the hook if it goes wrong, not purely because the reading and reasoning is intrinsically harder than lots of lower-paid work.

Second, what's hard for humans and what's hard for AI systems are just pretty different. This is the Moravec's paradox point. Lots of things humans find easy and therefore pay little for, like physical manipulation, navigating messy real-world environments, or sustaining coherent work over a long time with lots of context, are things models have historically been bad at. Meanwhile, things that take humans years of training, like recalling a huge body of specialized knowledge or writing certain kinds of code, can be comparatively easy for models. So the human difficulty ordering and the AI difficulty ordering don't line up neatly.

Third, the price of a task bundles together a lot of sub-skills. A high-paid job might be mostly routine with a few hard judgment calls, and the price is set by those judgment calls. If you're trying to predict whether an AI can do the task, you really need to know which components are the bottleneck for the model, and the wage doesn't tell you that.

So in our work we've found it more useful to look at things like how long a task takes a skilled human to complete. That's not perfect either, but it seems to track AI difficulty more directly than price does, because it's closer to measuring how much sequential work and error correction the task requires. Market price can be a useful signal for thinking about economic impact, what's valuable to automate, but as a predictor of whether a model will succeed, I'd treat it as pretty noisy and potentially misleading.

r001.rationale: The response says human and AI difficulty orderings do not line up: tasks humans find easy may challenge models, while some highly trained intellectual tasks may be comparatively easy for them.

r002.rationale: It identifies physical manipulation, messy real-world navigation, and sustained work with context as areas where models have struggled, contrasting them with specialized knowledge and coding.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the intuition behind using market price is pretty reasonable on its face. If a task costs a lot for a human to do, that's usually because it requires a lot of expertise or a lot of time, and both of those seem like they should correlate with how hard it is for an AI. And there's something nice about it being an external, revealed-preference kind of signal rather than me just making up a difficulty rating.

But I think it breaks down in a bunch of ways once you look at it closely. The first is that what humans are expensive at and what AI systems are expensive at are just different things. A lot of the price of human labor is tied up in things like how many years of training a person needs, how scarce that credential is, how much liability is attached to the work, how unpleasant it is, or how much of it is coordination and trust rather than the cognitive core of the task. A radiologist read is expensive partly because of the cognitive skill, but also because of medical school, licensing, malpractice risk, and the fact that someone needs to be accountable. None of that transfers to a model. Conversely, there are things humans find trivially cheap, like certain kinds of physical manipulation or just maintaining a consistent picture of a situation over a long time, that models can be really bad at. So the price is measuring the human-specific cost structure, not some task-intrinsic difficulty.

The second thing is that market price is pretty sensitive to the supply of people who can do the task, which is a historical and institutional fact, not a fact about the task. If a field happens to have a lot of competition or a lot of practitioners, prices get driven down even if the work is genuinely hard. And the reverse, where something is expensive because it's gated, not because it's hard.

The third issue, and the one I actually care about most for evaluation purposes, is that most tasks you'd want to measure aren't cleanly priced at all. You can get a rough number for "how much would a contractor charge to build this feature," but for the kind of long-horizon, messy, underspecified work that I think is most relevant for understanding AI capabilities, there isn't really a market. You end up having to imagine a counterfactual contractor and estimate what they'd charge, and at that point you've smuggled all your judgment back in, just with a dollar sign on it that makes it look more objective than it is.

So I don't think price is useless. It's a decent sanity check, and it's correlated with the things we care about. I just don't want to lean on it as the primary axis, because I think it would systematically mislead you about where AI is going to be strong and where it's going to be surprisingly weak. I'd rather try to measure the thing more directly, like how long it actually takes a competent person, or how the task decomposes, and treat price as one noisy input among several.

r001.rationale: The response says human and AI systems have different capability profiles and explains that prices reflect human-specific costs, while some tasks cheap for people can be difficult for models.

r002.rationale: The response discusses long-horizon, messy, underspecified tasks and model difficulty maintaining a consistent picture, but does not identify agency or sensitivity to messiness as a more plausible bottleneck than extensive human intellectual training.

astra-6.text:
Well, the price of a task reflects a lot more than how hard it is. It reflects how many people have the relevant skills, what their other opportunities are, and how much demand there is for the work. So even for humans, it’s not a clean measure of difficulty.

And then there’s a separate issue, which is that what’s hard for humans isn’t necessarily hard for AI. A task might command a high wage because it requires a lot of specialized knowledge, but that knowledge might be relatively easy for a model to acquire during training. Meanwhile, some fairly low-paid work involves physical skills or dealing with unfamiliar situations that are difficult for AI.

So I think prices can be useful for thinking about the economic value of automating a task. I’m much more cautious about using them to predict which tasks AI will be able to do.

r001.rationale: The response says human prices reflect factors beyond task difficulty and that tasks demanding specialized human knowledge may be easier for AI, while some lower-paid physical or unfamiliar tasks are harder for it. This clearly describes a mismatch between human and AI capabilities.

r002.rationale: The response mentions physical skills and unfamiliar situations as difficult for AI, but does not identify agency or sensitivity to task messiness as the more plausible current bottleneck.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the price of a task tells you about a bunch of things besides how difficult it is for an AI. It reflects how scarce the relevant human skills are, how much people want the task done, and how the work is organized. And the things that make a task hard for humans aren’t necessarily the things that make it hard for models.

So a task might be expensive because it requires a lot of specialized knowledge, which a model could potentially acquire during training. Meanwhile, something humans do cheaply and almost without thinking could be quite difficult for an AI. Price might still be a useful signal, but I’d be cautious about treating it as a general measure of difficulty or expecting AI capabilities to progress neatly from low-paid tasks to high-paid ones.

r001.rationale: It explains that what makes work difficult for humans may differ from what makes it difficult for AI, so human prices are not a general measure of AI capability.

r002.rationale: It contrasts specialized knowledge with tasks humans do cheaply, but does not identify agency or sensitivity to task messiness as a more plausible AI bottleneck.
